belief: I'm a burden now that I can't work.
origins: Illness, injury, disability, or age can limit work, and with it independence and income. Receiving care, relying on family, or needing help with money can feel like a burden to others. If we were always the strong one, being on the receiving side can be painful. The thought “They would be better off without me” can grow in the dark.
teaches: Paul says that the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable. We who are strong ought to bear with the weak, and we are to bear one another’s burdens. The psalmist prays, “Do not discard me in my old age; do not forsake me when my strength fails,” and God answers, “I have made you, and I will carry you.” Receiving care is part of how the body of Christ works. A person who cannot work still holds a place in the family and in God’s heart.
self_statements: My family would be better off without me.
I am just a drain on everyone.
I used to contribute and now I cannot.
I am a weight on those I love.
I should not need so much.
errors: Assuming that my family sees me as a burden.
Believing that I am either productive or a burden.
Feeling like a burden and concluding that I am.
questions: What have my family members actually said or done?
What do I give to my family that is not work, such as love, prayer, wisdom, or presence?
If my spouse or parent were in my place, would I see them as a burden?
What does Scripture say about those who seem weaker?
What would it mean to receive care graciously?
Who could I talk to about how I feel?
truth: Needing help does not make me a burden. In the body of Christ the weaker parts are indispensable, and in my family I am loved for who I am. I can receive care with grace and keep giving what I can, such as love, prayer, and presence.
hw_truths: I am loved for who I am, not what I do.
Receiving care is part of life together.
I still have gifts to give.
I can accept help with grace.
log: Each day, write one non-work thing you gave to someone, such as a prayer, a listening ear, or a word of thanks.
actions: Ask, “What does my being here mean to you?” and listen.
Write ten ways you contribute that do not require work.
Practice receiving help with gratitude instead of apology.
If heavy thoughts continue, speak to a pastor, counselor, or doctor, and if you ever feel unsafe, contact a crisis line right away.
prayer: Father, You carry me. Quiet the thought that I am a burden. Help me receive care gracefully, give what I can, and remember that I am loved by You and by those around me. Amen.
hw_questions: What have my loved ones actually said?
What do I give that is not work?
How would I view someone else in my place?
What does Scripture say about the weaker parts?
How can I receive help gracefully?
name_example: Sarah can write: “The parts that seem weaker are indispensable, so I am not a burden.”
